final_proof:
Write n·1_R for the additive integer multiple of 1_R (so for n<0 it means −((-n)·1_R)). We first establish the assertion that does not require any condition on zero divisors. For all m,n∈Z, the laws for integer multiples in the additive group of R give g(m+n)=g(m)+g(n). Repeated distributivity, first for nonnegative m,n and then the rule (−x)y=−(xy)=x(−y), gives (m·1_R)(n·1_R)=mn·1_R. Hence g(mn)=g(m)g(n), and g(1)=1_R. Thus g is a ring homomorphism.

Its image is precisely S. Indeed, im(g)={n·1_R:n∈Z} is a subring of R and contains 1_R, so the subring S generated by 1_R is contained in im(g). Conversely, every subring containing 1_R is closed under addition and additive inverses, and therefore contains n·1_R for every n∈Z. In particular S contains im(g). Thus S=im(g), and g:Z→S is surjective (and hence is an epimorphism).

Now assume that R has no proper zero divisors, in the sense that xy=0_R implies x=0_R or y=0_R, and, as is implicit when the claim calls g nonzero, assume 1_R≠0_R. Let f:Z→R be any ring homomorphism; it need not initially be assumed to preserve unity. Put e=f(1). Additivity determines f completely: f(n)=n·e for every n∈Z. Multiplicativity gives e²=f(1)²=f(1)=e, and hence e(e−1_R)=0_R. The zero-divisor hypothesis yields e=0_R or e−1_R=0_R. In the first case f is the zero homomorphism, while in the second e=1_R and f(n)=n·1_R=g(n) for every n. Therefore g is the unique nonzero ring homomorphism Z→R. (If ring homomorphisms are defined to preserve unity, the same uniqueness follows immediately.)

It remains to determine the kernel. Since ker(g) is an ideal of Z, there is a unique integer m≥0 such that ker(g)=mZ; when the kernel is nonzero, m is its least positive element. If m=0, then ker(g)=(0), and the first isomorphism theorem, together with im(g)=S, gives Z≅S; equivalently, g is an isomorphism from Z onto S.

Suppose instead that m>0. Since 1_R≠0_R, we cannot have m=1. We claim that m is prime. If it were composite, write m=ab with integers 1<a<m and 1<b<m. The minimality of m would imply a,b∉ker(g), so a·1_R and b·1_R would both be nonzero. But

(a·1_R)(b·1_R)=ab·1_R=m·1_R=g(m)=0_R,

contradicting the absence of proper zero divisors. Hence m=p for some prime p. Again by the first isomorphism theorem, S=im(g)≅Z/ker(g)=Z/pZ, which is a field.

Strictly speaking, because ker(g) is a subset of Z, the ideals in the dichotomy are the ideals (0) and (p) of Z, not principal ideals of R. Also, the kernel dichotomy must be read under the no-proper-zero-divisors hypothesis. If it is intended without that hypothesis, it is false: for R=Z/6Z with its usual unity, g is the quotient map and ker(g)=6Z, which is neither (0) nor (p) for a prime p. The unconditional corrected statement is ker(g)=mZ and S≅Z/mZ for some m≥0. Finally, if the zero ring 1_R=0_R is allowed, then g is zero and ker(g)=Z=(1); thus the phrase “unique nonzero homomorphism” also necessarily presupposes a nonzero ring.
